Description:
GHRP-6 (Growth Hormone-Releasing Peptide 6) is a synthetic hexapeptide and one of the first compounds shown to act as a growth hormone secretagogue in preclinical models. It binds the growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHS-R1a), the same receptor later identified as the target of the endogenous hormone ghrelin. Heartland Bio Labs supplies GHRP-6 for laboratory research in 5mg and 10mg vials, independently tested for purity and identity.

What GHRP-6 is

GHRP-6 came out of the structure-activity work on synthetic enkephalin analogues in the late 1970s and early 1980s, which found that small peptides with D-amino acid substitutions could trigger growth hormone release through a pathway separate from GHRH. Its sequence is His-D-Trp-Ala-Trp-D-Phe-Lys-NH2. The two D-residues make it far more resistant to enzymatic breakdown than a natural hexapeptide, which is why it remained a standard reference compound long after newer secretagogues appeared.

Because GHRP-6 was characterised years before ghrelin was discovered in 1999, much of the early receptor pharmacology for GHS-R1a was worked out with it. It is still used as a comparison agonist in research on ghrelin signalling, pituitary somatotroph function and the hypothalamic regulation of feeding behaviour in animal models, where it shows a pronounced ghrelin-like effect on appetite signalling.

GHRP-6 compared with related compounds

GHRP-6 is the first-generation member of the GHRP family. GHRP-2 was developed from it and is the more potent secretagogue per milligram in most published models, with a smaller effect on appetite signalling. Ipamorelin is a later pentapeptide valued for its selectivity: it acts on the same receptor with little effect on cortisol or prolactin in animal studies. GHRP-6 remains the choice when a protocol needs the classic reference agonist, or specifically wants the ghrelin-like feeding response that the newer compounds were designed to reduce. Secretagogues are often studied alongside GHRH analogues such as CJC-1295, since the two pathways act on the pituitary through different receptors.

MOTS-c (Mitochondrial Open reading frame of the Twelve S rRNA type-c) is a 16-amino acid peptide encoded not in the nucleus but in the mitochondrial genome, within the gene for 12S ribosomal RNA. It belongs to a small class of mitochondria-derived peptides and is studied as a signal by which mitochondria communicate with the rest of the cell. Heartland Bio Labs supplies MOTS-c for laboratory research in 10mg vials, independently tested for purity and identity.

What MOTS-c is

MOTS-c was first described in 2015 by researchers at the University of Southern California, who found a short open reading frame inside the mitochondrial 12S rRNA gene that codes for a functional peptide. Its sequence is MRWQEMGYIFYPRKLR. That discovery widened the idea of what the mitochondrial genome encodes, which had long been thought to be limited to 13 proteins of the respiratory chain plus the RNAs needed to make them.

Preclinical research on MOTS-c centres on cellular energy metabolism. In cell and animal models it has been linked to the folate cycle and to activation of AMPK, the cell's main energy sensor, which is why it is often studied alongside compounds such as AICAR. Later work reported that under metabolic stress MOTS-c moves into the nucleus and influences the expression of stress-response genes, making it a model for retrograde mitochondrial-to-nuclear signalling. It is also studied in research on ageing, exercise physiology and insulin sensitivity in rodent models.

AOD-9604 is a synthetic 16-amino acid peptide based on the C-terminal region of human growth hormone (residues 177–191), with a tyrosine added at the N-terminus. It was developed to study the part of the growth hormone molecule associated with fat metabolism in isolation from the rest of the hormone. Heartland Bio Labs supplies AOD-9604 for laboratory research in 2mg, 5mg and 10mg vials, independently tested for purity and identity.

What AOD-9604 is

Growth hormone has many effects, and in the 1990s researchers at Monash University in Australia set out to separate its effect on fat tissue from the rest. Work on fragments of the hormone showed that the C-terminal stretch, residues 177 to 191, carried much of the lipolytic activity seen in animal models. AOD-9604 is a modified version of that fragment: Tyr-Leu-Arg-Ile-Val-Gln-Cys-Arg-Ser-Val-Glu-Gly-Ser-Cys-Gly-Phe, with a disulfide bridge between the two cysteines.

What makes AOD-9604 useful in research is what it does not do. In preclinical studies it showed effects on lipolysis and lipogenesis in adipose tissue without the growth-promoting effects of the full hormone, and without raising IGF-1. That makes it a tool for studying adipocyte biology and fat metabolism pathways separately from growth hormone receptor signalling as a whole. It has also been studied in cartilage and connective tissue models.
